Chapter 7

Budgeting, Costs, and Vendors

预算、成本与供应商

Budgeting is something that most of us never expected to think about as engineering leaders. Most engineering leaders perceive themselves as making technical decisions, and they see finance and budget decisions as “business problems.” Well, solving those “business problems” is how we get the people and resources we need to deliver products and services to our customers (also in the business) and, significantly, help us understand how we get paid, plan for our future needs, and how the business functions. Budgeting is also an anchor in a chaotic environment. It dovetails into your planning and prioritization process to help you understand the resources needed to deliver on your plans.

做工程领导，大多数人从没料到自己还要操心预算。多数工程领导觉得自己是做技术决策的，把财务和预算决策看成“业务部门的事”。但实际上，解决这些“业务问题”，正是我们获取人力与资源、向客户交付产品和服务（客户也在业务侧）的方式，而且更重要的是，它帮我们理解公司靠什么赚钱、如何为未来需求做规划、以及业务究竟是如何运转的。在混乱的环境里，预算也是一根定盘针。它与你的规划和优先级排定过程紧密衔接，帮你看清交付计划到底需要哪些资源。

Budgeting is not just crunching numbers (although I guarantee you that you’ll see a lot of spreadsheets; there is nothing that accountants like more than spreadsheets). Budgeting is a strategic process that enables you and your organization to anticipate challenges, seize opportunities, and maintain competitive advantages. By systematically budgeting for people and resources, you, your team, and your organization can create a roadmap that bridges the gap between your current position and your desired future state.

预算不只是捏数字（不过我可以保证，你会看到大量电子表格——会计师最喜欢的东西就是电子表格）。预算是一个战略性流程，让你和你的组织能够预判挑战、抓住机会、保持竞争优势。通过系统性地为人力和资源做预算，你、你的团队和你的组织就能画出一张路线图，弥合“你现在在哪里”与“你想去往何方”之间的差距。

In this chapter, we explain why budgeting is necessary and discuss the basics of budgeting and cost management (as the other side of budgeting is working out what you’ve overspent on). And we discuss the procurement of products and services and how to deal with vendors. It’s important to note that neither of us is an accountant (nor a lawyer nor medical professional), so this is a layperson’s guide to understanding the basics of budgeting and costs. This is not professional financial planning or legal advice, and you should always work on budgets and costs with someone who actually knows what they are doing, like your chief financial officer or finance team.

本章我们会解释为什么预算必不可少，并讨论预算与成本管理的基础（预算的另一面，就是搞清楚你在哪些地方超支了）。我们还会讨论产品与服务的采购，以及如何与供应商打交道。需要说明的是，我们俩都不是会计师（也不是律师或医生），所以这只是一本帮你理解预算与成本基础的外行指南。它不构成专业的财务规划或法律建议；在处理预算和成本时，你永远应该和真正懂行的人一起做，比如你的首席财务官或财务团队。

Why Budgeting Matters

为什么预算很重要

Throughout this book, we’ve discussed that doing something is (almost) always better than doing nothing. This applies doubly to budgeting. You might think budgeting is just about controlling costs or allocating money, but it’s the foundation of turning your grand visions into reality. Think of it as the bridge between “Wouldn’t it be cool if we…” and “We actually did it!”

贯穿全书我们都在说：做些什么，几乎总是比什么都不做强。这条原则在预算上加倍成立。你可能以为预算只是控制开支或分钱，但它其实是把宏大愿景变成现实的基石。把它想成一座桥——一端是“要是我们能……那该多酷”，另一端是“我们真的做到了！”

Strategic Alignment

战略对齐

Let’s start with aligning spending with your mission: strategic alignment. This isn’t just corporate speak for “ensuring everything lines up.” It’s about ensuring that your spending matches your stated priorities. If you say customer experience is your top priority, but your budget shows that all your resources are going to internal tools, well…you might want to rethink either your strategy or your spending.

我们先从“让开支与使命对齐”说起：这就是战略对齐。它不只是“确保一切都对得上”的企业黑话，而是要确保你的钱花在你宣称的优先级上。如果你嘴上说客户体验是头等大事，预算却显示所有资源都投给了内部工具——那你大概得重新想想，要么改战略，要么改开支。

In Practice: April’s Story

实战：April 的故事

At PixelCurl, April faced this misalignment head on when reviewing the StudioOps Q1 budget. Despite claiming “collaboration and mentorship” as top priorities after losing two junior engineers to frustration, the budget told a different story: $15,000 allocated to individual JetBrains licenses for each engineer, $5,000 for personal productivity tracking tools, but zero dollars for pair programming tools like Tuple or CodeTogether. The “team building” line item turned out to be a lonely $500 for “quarterly pizza.” So, April reallocated: she cut the productivity tracking tools that nobody actually used, negotiated a team license for a pair programming tool ($8,000), instituted weekly team lunches ($600 a month), and set aside $10,000 for a proper code review tool.

在 PixelCurl，April 审核 StudioOps 第一季度预算时，直接撞上了这种错位。在因挫败而走了两名初级工程师之后，公司嘴上把“协作与导师制”列为头等优先，预算却讲着另一个故事：给每位工程师单独买 JetBrains 许可证花了 15,000 美元，个人效率追踪工具花了 5,000 美元，而 Tuple、CodeTogether 这类结对编程工具一分钱没有。“团队建设”那一项，可怜巴巴地只有 500 美元，备注是“季度披萨”。于是 April 重新分配：砍掉没人真用的效率追踪工具，谈下一个结对编程工具的团队许可证（8,000 美元），设立每周团队午餐（每月 600 美元），并留出 10,000 美元买一套正经的代码评审工具。

We need to develop clear frameworks for deciding what’s worth investing in. This isn’t about creating complex scoring systems (but if that’s your thing, go for it); it’s about having honest conversations about what matters most. You’ll need to balance your short-term needs (keeping the lights on) with your long-term dreams (becoming the next tech unicorn). And yes, you’ll need to coordinate across different teams—finance can’t live in a bubble, and neither can engineering.

我们需要建立清晰的框架，来判断什么值得投资。这不是要搞一套复杂的打分系统（不过如果你好这口，尽管去搞）；而是要就“什么最重要”展开坦诚的对话。你得在短期需求（让灯亮着）和长期梦想（成为下一个科技独角兽）之间取得平衡。而且没错，你需要跨团队协调——财务不能活在气泡里，工程也不能。

Cost Management

成本管理

Cost management isn’t just about finding the cheapest option for everything (though your chief financial officer might wish it was). It’s about understanding the actual relationship between spending and value. We need to get clever about how we classify and track costs. Fixed costs are like rent—they don’t care if you had a good or bad month; they’re showing up either way. Variable costs are more like your coffee habits—they scale with your activity level (and stress level, let’s be honest).

成本管理不只是凡事找最便宜的选项（虽然你的 CFO 可能巴不得如此）。它是要理解开支与价值之间的真实关系。我们得聪明地对成本进行分类和追踪。固定成本就像房租——你这个月生意好坏它都不在乎，反正照收不误。变动成本则更像你的喝咖啡习惯——它随你的活跃度（说实话，也随你的压力水平）水涨船高。

Understanding the Income Side of the Equation

理解等式的收入端

While engineering leaders don’t typically own revenue targets, understanding how your costs relate to income transforms you from a cost center to a strategic partner. This is where unit economics come into play, and they’re simpler than they sound. There are some key concepts you’ll hear a lot about in unit economics, especially if you sell products and services to others:

虽然工程领导通常不背营收指标，但理解成本与收入的关系，能让你从一个“成本中心”变成“战略伙伴”。这就是单位经济模型（unit economics）发挥作用的地方，而它其实比听起来简单。在单位经济模型里，有几个关键概念你会反复听到，尤其是当你向外部销售产品和服务时：

Cost of goods sold (COGS). COGS represents the direct costs of delivering your product or service. For a software as a service (SaaS) company, this includes infrastructure costs, third-party service fees, and support costs directly tied to serving customers. If you’re running $50,000 monthly in Amazon Web Services (AWS) costs to serve 1,000 customers, that’s $50 per customer in infrastructure COGS. This number matters because it directly impacts your gross margin: the percentage of revenue left after subtracting COGS.

销货成本（COGS）。COGS 指交付产品或服务所产生的直接成本。对一家 SaaS（软件即服务）公司而言，它包括基础设施成本、第三方服务费，以及与服务客户直接相关的支持成本。如果你每月花 50,000 美元的 AWS（亚马逊云）费用来服务 1,000 个客户，那每个客户摊到的基础设施 COGS 就是 50 美元。这个数字之所以重要，是因为它直接影响你的毛利率（gross margin）：即收入减去 COGS 之后剩下的百分比。

Customer acquisition cost (CAC). CAC is what it costs to land a new customer. While marketing and sales often own most of this, engineering contributes through the features and performance that make the product sellable. If your sales team is spending $5,000 to acquire each enterprise customer because your product lacks key features that competitors have, that missing functionality has a real dollar impact.

客户获取成本（CAC）。CAC 指拿下一个新客户要花多少钱。虽然这块通常由市场和销售主导，但工程部门也有份——正是那些让产品卖得动的功能和性能在做贡献。如果因为你的产品缺少竞品已有的关键功能，销售团队每拿下一个企业客户就要花 5,000 美元，那这个缺失的功能就有实打实的金钱代价。

Lifetime value (LTV). LTV represents the total revenue a customer generates over their relationship with you. Engineering has a direct impact on LTV through product quality, reliability, and feature development. A bug that causes 10% monthly churn doesn’t just affect your bug metrics; if your average customer pays $1,000 per month and churns after 10 months instead of 12, you’ve lost $2,000 in LTV.

客户终身价值（LTV）。LTV 指一个客户在与你合作的整个周期里贡献的总收入。工程部门通过产品质量、可靠性和功能开发直接影响 LTV。一个导致每月流失率上升 10% 的 bug，影响的不只是你的 bug 指标；如果你的客户平均每月付 1,000 美元，本可以留 12 个月结果只留了 10 个月就走，那你就在 LTV 上损失了 2,000 美元。

Gross margin. Gross margin is where it all comes together: (revenue – COGS) ÷ revenue. This percentage tells you how much money you have to cover everything else: salaries, office space, and that fancy coffee machine. Engineering teams that understand gross margin make better decisions. Should you optimize that database query that’s consuming 20% of your infrastructure costs? If you’re at 70% gross margin and trying to reach 80%, that optimization might be more valuable than the new feature that your product manager wants.

毛利率。毛利率是所有东西汇聚之处：（收入 – COGS）÷ 收入。这个百分比告诉你，手里还剩多少钱去覆盖其他一切开支：工资、办公场地，还有那台高端咖啡机。理解毛利率的工程团队会做出更好的决策。那个吃掉你 20% 基础设施成本的数据库查询，要不要优化？如果你现在毛利率 70%、想冲到 80%，那这次优化可能比产品经理想要的新功能更有价值。

In Practice: April’s Story

实战：April 的故事

April discovered the connection of LTV at PixelCurl when analyzing why the StudioOps team kept missing deadlines. The sales team revealed that they were discounting heavily (reducing LTV) because competitors ship features more quickly. The product team reported that customer churn will spike after major outages (further reducing LTV). Suddenly, the “cost” of her team’s velocity became quantifiable; the company was losing $30,000 per month in churned revenue because bugs took too long to fix. This became a key input into how April builds her budget, prioritizes her work, and decides where to allocate her headcount.

在 PixelCurl，April 分析 StudioOps 团队为什么总赶不上截止日期时，发现了 LTV 的这种关联。销售团队透露，因为竞品发功能更快，他们不得不大幅打折（压低了 LTV）。产品团队则报告说，每次重大故障之后客户流失都会飙升（进一步压低 LTV）。突然间，她团队“交付速度”的代价变得可量化了：因为 bug 修得太慢，公司每月在流失的收入上损失 30,000 美元。这成了 April 做预算、排优先级、决定把 HC（人头编制）投到哪里的关键输入。

Making Unit Economics Work for Prioritization

让单位经济模型服务于优先级排定

Once you understand these metrics, every technical decision becomes a business decision. That refactoring project that reduces infrastructure costs by 30% directly improves gross margin. The authentication feature that enables enterprise sales could double your LTV. The performance improvement that reduces support tickets lowers your cost to serve each customer.

一旦你理解了这些指标，每个技术决策就都变成了业务决策。那个把基础设施成本砍掉 30% 的重构项目，直接提升了毛利率。那个让企业级销售成为可能的认证功能，可能让你的 LTV 翻倍。那个减少了支持工单的性能优化，降低了你服务每个客户的成本。

Consider how this changes conversations around prioritization. Instead of arguing whether Feature A or Feature B is more important, you can discuss the following:

想想这会如何改变围绕优先级的讨论。你们不必再争论功能 A 和功能 B 谁更重要，而是可以这样谈：

  • Feature A reduces infrastructure costs by $10,000 a month, improving gross margin by 2%.

    功能 A 每月减少 10,000 美元基础设施成本，把毛利率提升 2%。

  • Feature B enables enterprise-tier pricing, increasing average LTV from $10,000 to $25,000.

    功能 B 让企业级定价成为可能，把平均 LTV 从 10,000 美元提升到 25,000 美元。

This framework also helps justify engineering investments. If you need to hire a new DevOps engineer, frame it as, “This hire will reduce our infrastructure COGS by 25% through optimization, improving gross margin from 72% to 76%, which adds $2 million to our valuation at standard SaaS multiples.”

这个框架也帮你为工程投资争取理由。如果你要招一个新的 DevOps 工程师，可以这样表述：“这个人入职后，会通过优化把基础设施 COGS 降低 25%，把毛利率从 72% 提升到 76%，按 SaaS 行业的标准估值倍数，这会给公司估值增加 200 万美元。”

Many people think that cost management is about cutting costs, but it’s actually about understanding how costs behave in your organization. Sometimes, spending more in one area can save you money overall. It’s like buying a good pair of boots—they might cost more upfront, but they’ll last longer than cheap ones. We must balance immediate savings against long-term value, which requires tactical thinking and strategic vision. We’ll discuss cost management in the dedicated section later in this chapter.

很多人以为成本管理就是砍成本，但它其实是要理解成本在你的组织里是怎么运作的。有时候在一个地方多花钱，整体上反而更省。这就像买一双好靴子—— upfront 贵一点，但比便宜货耐穿得多。我们必须在眼前省下的钱和长期价值之间取得平衡，这既需要战术思考，也需要战略眼光。本章后面有专门一节展开讨论成本管理。

All credit for this metaphor to Terry Pratchett’s Sam Vimes “Boots” theory of socioeconomic unfairness.

这个比喻完全出自 Terry Pratchett 笔下 Sam Vimes 的“靴子理论”——关于社会经济不公的那个著名论述。

Risk Mitigation

风险缓释

If there’s one thing we’ve learned, the universe loves a good plot twist. Risk mitigation through budgeting is your way of saying, “Nice try, universe, but we thought of that.” This isn’t just about having a rainy-day fund (though that’s not a bad idea). It’s about understanding what could go wrong and having a plan and the resources to deal with it.

如果说我们学到了一件事，那就是：宇宙最爱来个神转折。通过预算做风险缓释，就是你对宇宙说：“想得美，但这一我们早就料到了。”这不只是存一笔应急钱（虽然这主意不坏）；而是要想清楚可能出什么岔子，并且备好应对的计划和资源。

We need to consider financial risks (e.g., What if our largest customer leaves?), operational risks (e.g., What if our primary database server fails?), and strategic risks (e.g., What if our competitor renders our product obsolete?). Your budget must include provisions for addressing these risks, whether through direct investment in solutions or maintaining contingency funds.

我们要考虑财务风险（比如：最大的客户走了怎么办？）、运营风险（比如：主数据库服务器挂了怎么办？）、以及战略风险（比如：竞品把我们的产品淘汰了怎么办？）。你的预算必须包含应对这些风险的准备，无论是直接投资于解决方案，还是预留应急资金。

Performance Monitoring

绩效监控

Remember when we talked about measuring things? Budgeting gives us another lens for this. We need to track financial and operational metrics, but the key is that they must provide us with useful insights. Vanity metrics are like vanity muscles; they might look good, but they’re not helping you win the race.

还记得我们聊过“度量”这件事吗？预算给了我们又一个视角。我们要追踪财务和运营指标，但关键在于这些指标必须能带来有用的洞察。虚荣指标（vanity metrics）就像健美先生练出来的炫耀肌——看着好看，并不能帮你赢得比赛。

We want leading indicators (early warning signs) and lagging indicators (confirmation that what we did worked). Think of it as a weather forecast versus looking out the window; both are useful, but for different reasons.

我们想要先行指标（预警信号）和滞后指标（确认我们做的事奏效了）。把它想成天气预报和走到窗边往外看的区别：两者都有用，但用处不同。

Resource Optimization

资源优化

Resource optimization sounds fancy, but it’s about making smart choices with limited resources (and resources are always limited, even at the biggest companies). This isn’t just about money; it’s about people, technology, time, and all the other things that help you get stuff done.

资源优化听上去很高级，说白了就是在有限资源下做聪明的选择（而资源永远是有限的，哪怕在最大的公司也一样）。这不只是钱的事；它关乎人、技术、时间，以及所有帮你把活干完的东西。

If Chapter 6 taught us anything, it’s that prioritization is the art of deciding what to do when you can’t do everything. Budgeting is simply prioritization with dollar signs attached. The impact-versus-effort matrix we use to determine which user stories to tackle next can also scale up to budgeting decisions. Should we hire another engineer or invest in better tools? Which option sits in the high-value, low-effort quadrant of our organizational priorities?

如果说第 6 章教会了我们什么，那就是：优先级排定是一门艺术——当你做不完所有事时，决定先做什么。预算不过是挂上美元符号的优先级排定。我们用来决定下一个做哪个用户故事的“影响 vs. 投入”矩阵，同样可以放大到预算决策上。是再招一个工程师，还是投资更好的工具？哪个选项落在我们组织优先级里的“高价值、低投入”象限？

Think of your budget as your backlog at the company level. Just as you manage a product backlog with user stories, acceptance criteria, and regular grooming sessions, your budget requires the same disciplined approach but with broader impact. When you estimate a user story at two weeks of engineering effort, you’re implicitly allocating budget; those two weeks represent salary, infrastructure costs, and opportunity costs. When you decide to tackle technical debt instead of new features, you’re

把你的预算想象成公司层面的 backlog。就像你用用户故事、验收标准和定期梳理会来管理产品 backlog 一样，你的预算也需要同样有纪律的做法，只是影响面更大。当你把一个用户故事估成两周工程工作量时，你其实就是在暗分配预算；那两周代表着工资、基础设施成本和机会成本。当你决定去处理技术债而不是做新功能时，你就是在做一个资源优化决策——它同时影响你的 sprint 计划和季度预算。

— 原书第 147 页 —

making a resource optimization decision that affects both your sprint planning and your quarterly budget.

（接上文）这个决策同时影响你的 sprint 计划和季度预算。

We need clear criteria for making trade-offs, and these criteria should mirror your prioritization framework. Remember how we categorize work into features, bugs, technical debt, and maintenance? Your budget needs the same balance. Allocating 100% of resources to new features while ignoring technical debt is like planning sprints without ever addressing your bug backlog; it might work for a sprint or two, but eventually, the accumulated debt will force your hand.

我们需要清晰的标准来做权衡，而这些标准应当映照你的优先级框架。还记得我们怎么把工作分成功能、bug、技术债和维护四类吗？你的预算也需要同样的平衡。把 100% 资源都投给新功能、对技术债视而不见，就像排 sprint 却从不碰 bug backlog；撑得过一两个 sprint，但累积下来的债迟早会逼你还债。

The estimation challenges we discussed in Chapter 6 also scale up to budgeting. Just as we accept ±25% variance in early sprint estimates, your budget estimates for new initiatives will carry similar uncertainty. If there is a contractor that you think you need for three months, you should budget for four months. Similarly, for the infrastructure upgrade that is estimated at $50,000, have a conversation about what happens at $65,000. The same principles apply: acknowledge uncertainty, communicate it transparently, and narrow the variance as you learn more.

我们在第 6 章讨论过的估算难题，同样会放大到预算上。正如我们接受早期 sprint 估算有 ±25% 的误差，你对新计划的预算估算也会带着类似的不确定性。如果你估计需要一个承包商三个月，那就按四个月做预算。同样，那个预估 50,000 美元的基础设施升级，也该聊一聊：如果花到 65,000 美元会怎样？原则是一样的：承认不确定性、透明地把它说出来，并随着了解加深不断收窄误差。

In Practice: April’s Story

实战：April 的故事

At PixelCurl, April sees this connection clearly when she realizes that her team’s inability to accurately estimate story points has a direct impact on her ability to budget for the coming quarter. If the team consistently underestimates effort by 30%, her headcount planning will be off by the same margin. She starts treating budget planning sessions as extended sprint planning, using the same impact-versus-effort discussions but adding dollar amounts to each axis.

在 PixelCurl，April 清楚地看到了这种关联：她意识到团队没法准确估算故事点，直接影响了她为下季度做预算的能力。如果团队一贯把工作量低估 30%，她的人头编制规划也会偏差同样多。于是她开始把预算规划会当作延长版的 sprint 规划，用同样的“影响 vs. 投入”讨论，只是在每个轴上都加上了美元金额。

These decisions need to consider both immediate needs and long-term implications. Should we upgrade our infrastructure now or wait until next quarter? Apply the same logic you use for technical debt: what’s the interest rate on this particular debt? If waiting costs you more in inefficiency, incidents, or lost opportunities than the upgrade itself, the decision becomes clear. Your budget is your organization’s way of keeping score on these prioritization decisions, ensuring that your resource allocation matches your stated priorities.

这些决策既要考虑眼前需求，也要考虑长远影响。现在就升级基础设施，还是等到下季度？用你处理技术债的同一套逻辑：这笔“债”的利率是多少？如果等待让你在低效、事故或错失机会上付出的代价超过升级本身，那决策就很清楚了。你的预算，就是组织为这些优先级决策记分的方式，确保资源分配与你宣称的优先级一致。

Stakeholder Management

干系人管理

Your budget isn’t just a planning tool; it’s a communication tool. It tells investors and leadership what you’re prioritizing, shows employees where the company is heading, and demonstrates to customers that you’re investing in their needs. Transparency in your budgeting process builds trust, but it needs the right kind of transparency. Nobody needs to know how much you spend on coffee filters, but they should know about significant investments in new technology or capabilities.

你的预算不只是规划工具，也是沟通工具。它告诉投资人和领导你在优先做什么，让员工看到公司要往哪走，向客户证明你在为他们的需求投入。预算过程的透明度能建立信任，但需要的是恰当的透明。没人需要知道你咖啡滤纸花了多少钱，但他们应当知道你在新技术或新能力上的重大投资。

— 原书第 148 页 —

Innovation and Growth

创新与增长

Here’s where budgeting gets exciting (yes, really). Innovation and growth initiatives need explicit funding—they rarely happen by accident. We must set aside resources for both incremental improvements (enhancing our existing products) and transformative innovation (creating entirely new products).

到这儿，预算就开始有意思了（真的）。创新和增长类计划需要明确的资金——它们极少凭空发生。我们必须为两类事情都留出资源：渐进式改进（增强现有产品）和颠覆式创新（创造全新产品）。

This is like planting a garden; some plants will give you tomatoes this summer, while others are trees that won’t bear fruit for years. You need both, and your budget needs to reflect that.

这就像种菜园子：有些植物今年夏天就给你结番茄，另一些是要等好几年才结果的树。两者你都需要，而你的预算必须反映这一点。

Organizational Learning

组织学习

Every budgeting cycle is an opportunity to learn and improve. We should capture insights about what worked, what didn’t, and why. This isn’t just about getting better at budgeting—it’s about getting better at everything the budget supports.

每一轮预算周期都是一次学习和改进的机会。我们应当记录下：哪些奏效了、哪些没有、为什么。这不只是为了把预算做得更好——而是为了把预算所支撑的一切事情都做得更好。

Think of each budget cycle as an experiment, where some things will work better than expected, but others worse. The key is to learn from both and adjust accordingly.

把每一轮预算都当成一次实验：有些事会比预期更顺利，有些则不如预期。关键是从两者中都学习，并据此调整。

Competitive Advantage

竞争优势

Finally, remember that good budgeting can give you a competitive edge. It helps you respond more quickly to market changes, invest in the right capabilities at the right time, and maintain the flexibility to seize opportunities as they arise.

最后，请记住：好的预算能给你带来竞争优势。它帮你更快响应市场变化、在正确的时间投资正确的能力，并保持灵活性，机会一出现就能抓住。

Instead of just being about controlling spending, budgeting is about enabling success. It’s a tool that helps turn your strategy into actual results, and while it might not be the most exciting part of your job, getting it right makes all the exciting parts possible.

预算不只是控制开支，更是让成功成为可能的赋能手段。它是帮你把战略变成实际结果的工具。虽然它可能不是你工作中最刺激的部分，但把它做对，才让所有刺激的部分成为可能。

Finally, remember that you can always add processes to your budgeting, but it’s much harder to remove them. As we described in Chapter 6, when discussing agile practices: start simple, learn what works for your organization, and build from there. The goal is to create a budget that helps you achieve your goals while effectively managing risks and resources.

最后请记住：预算流程你随时能加，但要减掉就难多了。正如我们在第 6 章讨论敏捷实践时所说：从简单开始，摸清什么对自己的组织有效，再往上搭。目标是做出一份既能帮你达成目标、又能有效管理风险和资源的预算。

Understanding Cost Management

理解成本管理

Before you can build a budget, you need to understand what you’re spending and how you’re spending it. So, let’s talk about everyone’s favorite topic: costs! Okay, maybe not everyone’s favorite, but understanding costs is like having a good map when exploring new territory; it helps you know where you are, where you can go, and what obstacles might be in your way.

在做预算之前，你得先搞清楚自己在花什么钱、怎么花的。那我们就来聊聊大家最爱的话题：成本！好吧，也许不是每个人最爱，但理解成本就像探索新大陆时手里有张好地图：它帮你知道自己在哪、能往哪走、路上可能有什么障碍。

— 原书第 149 页 —

But the thing about costs is that they only tell half the story. To make truly strategic decisions, you need to understand how your costs relate to the value you’re creating. Think of your organization’s cost structure as a complex Lego creation, but one that needs to generate more value than it consumes. Some pieces are firmly locked in place (your fixed costs), while others can be easily swapped or adjusted (your variable costs). And critically, each piece should contribute to building something valuable enough that customers will pay for it. Understanding how these pieces fit together and how they connect to revenue is crucial for making smart decisions about your organization’s future.

但成本这东西只讲了故事的一半。要做出真正战略性的决策，你得理解成本与你正在创造的价值之间是什么关系。把组织的成本结构想象成一件复杂的乐高作品，但它必须创造出比它消耗掉的更多的价值。有些零件牢牢锁死在位置上（你的固定成本），另一些则可以轻松调换或调整（你的变动成本）。关键是，每一块零件都应当有助于拼出某个有价值到客户愿意为之付费的东西。理解这些零件如何拼在一起、又如何与收入相连，对组织未来的明智决策至关重要。

Fixed Costs: The Foundation

固定成本：地基

Fixed costs include factors like:

固定成本包括以下这些：

  • Your office

    你的办公场地

  • Permanent staff salaries

    正式员工的工资

  • Insurance premiums

    保险费

  • Core technology infrastructure

    核心技术基础设施

We need to manage these costs carefully. Too many fixed costs can make you rigid and inflexible, but too few might mean you lack the necessary infrastructure to grow. It’s a balancing act, and like most balancing acts, it’s trickier than it looks.

我们得小心管理这些成本。固定成本太多会让你僵硬、不灵活；但太少又可能意味着你缺乏成长所需的基础设施。这是一场平衡术，而像大多数平衡术一样，它看着简单，做起来比看起来难。

Variable Costs: The Flex Players

变动成本：灵活选手

Variable costs, like your coffee budget, go up when you’re busy and go down when you’re not. The most significant item for most tech teams is usage-based tech services, such as cloud services and SaaS. Managing variable costs involves striking a balance between efficiency and effectiveness. You could switch to the cheapest materials, but if your product falls apart, that’s not a win.

变动成本就像你的咖啡预算：忙的时候涨，闲的时候降。对大多数技术团队来说，最大的变动成本项是按用量计费的技术服务，比如云服务和 SaaS。管理变动成本，要在效率和效果之间取得平衡。你可以换成最便宜的材料，但如果产品因此散架，那就不算赢。

Step Costs: The Level-Up Costs

阶梯成本：升级成本

It’s worth highlighting step-up costs because not all costs grow linearly. Remember playing video games where you’d reach a new level and suddenly need better equipment? Step-up costs are like that. They jump up at certain thresholds. Moving to a higher tier of SaaS, opening a new office, or expanding your infrastructure are all step-up costs. Before jumping, you must be sure you’re ready or have at least considered the possibility of that next level.

值得特别拎出来说的是阶梯成本，因为并不是所有成本都线性增长。还记得打游戏升到新等级、突然就需要更好装备吗？阶梯成本就是这样：它在某个阈值上突然跳一档。升到更高一档的 SaaS、开新办公室、扩容基础设施，都是阶梯成本。在跳档之前，你必须确定自己准备好了，或者至少认真掂量过“下一级”意味着什么。

— 原书第 150 页 —

Who Pays?

谁来买单？

We also need to consider who owns the costs. In larger companies, this is an intricate dance. If one department consumes a service that might have people and infrastructure costs, do you bill that department? These are generally called direct costs. Some of them, like people, are usually easy to categorize and typically reasonably easy to allocate.

我们还要考虑谁来承担这些成本。在大公司里，这是一场复杂的舞蹈。如果某个部门消耗了一项服务，而这项服务背后有人员和基础设施成本，你要不要把账算到那个部门头上？这些通常叫直接成本。其中有些（比如人力）通常好分类，也比较容易分摊。

On the other hand, there are indirect costs, such as shared costs. A single customer likely consumes a percentage of your infrastructure spend, so you need to determine that percentage and who consumes what.

另一方面，还有间接成本，比如共享成本。单个客户大概只消耗了你基础设施支出的一定比例，所以你得算出这个比例，以及谁消耗了什么。

Even if you don’t bill a specific department or customer, it’s essential to understand who uses your services and what that costs. When budget time comes around, you must show that your investments have been worthwhile and that further investment, either continued or increased, is worth it.

就算你不向某个具体部门或客户收费，弄清楚谁在用你的服务、这要花多少钱，仍然至关重要。到了做预算的时候，你必须证明自己的投资是值得的，并且继续或加大投资也是值得的。

The Human Side of Cost Management

成本管理中有人的一面

People often forget that cost management is as much about people as it is about numbers. Having the right mentality is key. You should build a culture that considers costs. For example, choosing a new architecture that requires purchasing a new tool or platform, or incurring a step-up cost, will have an impact on expenditure. Your senior engineers should be able to consider that, even if it’s just an extension of capacity planning or performance estimation.

人们常常忘记：成本管理既关乎数字，也同样关乎人。拥有正确的心态是关键。你应当建立一种会把成本纳入考量的文化。比如，选一个新架构——而这需要购买新工具或新平台，或者触发一笔阶梯成本——就会影响支出。你的高级工程师应当能把这点考虑进去，哪怕它只是容量规划或性能估算的延伸。

Remember: just like with any other aspect of running an organization, the goal isn’t perfection; it’s continuous improvement. Start by understanding your costs, making informed decisions, and learning from and adjusting to them. And yes, sometimes that means admitting that the fancy coffee machine for the office was not the most strategic investment (but try taking it away now!).

请记住：和运营组织的其他方面一样，目标不是完美，而是持续改进。从理解你的成本开始，做出知情的决策，并从中学习、随之调整。是的，有时候这意味着你得承认：办公室那台高端咖啡机并不是最具战略意义的投资（不过现在再想把它搬走试试！）。

Creating and Managing a Budget

创建与管理预算

Let’s discuss creating and managing a budget. Much like planning a road trip, when creating a budget, you need to know where you’re starting from, where you want to go, and what resources you’ll need. In this section, we’ll break down how to create and manage a budget that works.

我们来聊聊怎么创建和管理预算。就像规划一次公路旅行，做预算时你得知道：从哪出发、要去哪、需要什么资源。本节我们会拆解：如何做出并管好一份真正管用的预算。

You may not have to do this alone. Many companies have finance teams that gather your input and turn it into actual financial plans. But even with a chief financial officer and a finance team, you are ultimately spending the budget, and you are responsible for ensuring that it gives you what you need and that you’re using it to plan.

你未必得一个人扛。很多公司有财务团队，他们收集你的输入，把它变成真正的财务计划。但哪怕有 CFO 和财务团队，最终花这笔预算的人是你，你也有责任确保它给你所需、并且你在用它来做规划。

— 原书第 151 页 —

Starting with History

从历史数据出发

It can be helpful to think of historical data as your organization’s diary. It tells you what happened, not what you think happened. We want to look back at least three years if possible (though in chaotic environments, sometimes yesterday feels like ancient history). We’re looking for revenue patterns that might show if your business has seasons or key customer dependencies; for example, many ecommerce companies see significantly increased variable costs around Black Friday and the holiday period as customer use increases. We need to understand expense trends to know where the money goes and identify those weird one-time incidents that pop up, like that office renovation that went way over budget.

把历史数据想象成组织的日记，会很有帮助。它记录的是实际发生了什么，而不是你以为发生了什么。如果可能，我们希望至少回看三年（不过在混乱的环境里，有时候昨天都像上古史）。我们要找的是收入规律，看看业务是否有季节性、是否依赖某些关键客户；比如，很多电商公司在黑色星期五和假日期间，随着用户使用量上升，变动成本会显著增加。我们要理解支出趋势，搞清楚钱花去了哪里，并揪出那些突然冒出来的奇怪一次性事件——比如那次远超预算的办公室装修。

When diving into historical data, we need the “what” (numbers) and the “why” (context). When thinking about that growth spike last year, consider whether it was because of your brilliant strategy, or if your competitor accidentally set their warehouse on fire. Context matters, and understanding the story behind the numbers is crucial for making good decisions.

钻研历史数据时，我们既需要“是什么”（数字），也需要“为什么”（背景）。想到去年那次增长尖峰时，要琢磨一下：是因为你的战略英明，还是竞品不小心把仓库点着了？背景很重要，理解数字背后的故事，对做出好决策至关重要。

Categorizing Expenses

给支出分类

Now, we break down our expenses into categories that make sense. If you’ve got a previous year’s budget, you already have an initial list to build on. Start with your people costs, as these are usually your most costly line item. Beyond just salaries (though those are big enough), we’re talking about the whole package: base pay that keeps the lights on at everyone’s home, variable compensation that rewards good performance, and benefits because health care isn’t free (speaking from a United States perspective). There are also expenses like training, conferences, and books, because we want our people to get better at what they do. You probably also want to factor in travel and expenses if your team is remote or travels to visit customers or other offices. Finally, consider entertainment expenses: office parties, mini golf days, or whatever floats your team’s boat.

现在我们把支出拆成有意义的类别。如果你有上一年的预算，就已经有了一份可以打底的初始清单。先从人力成本开始，因为它通常是你最大的支出项。不只是工资（虽然工资已经够大了），我们说的是整包：让每个人家里灯亮着的基本工资、奖励好绩效的浮动薪酬，还有福利——因为医疗不是免费的（这里是从美国视角说的）。还有培训、会议、买书之类的支出，因为我们希望团队成员在自己的领域越做越好。如果你的团队是远程的，或者要出差见客户、去其他办公室，大概还要把差旅算进去。最后，考虑一下团建娱乐开销：办公室派对、迷你高尔夫日，或者任何能让你团队嗨起来的活动。

Infrastructure is like your organization’s skeleton; you need it to stand up straight. This includes all your technology costs (sadly, the Cloud isn’t made of cloud or, more excitingly, candyfloss), physical space (if you still have an office), and equipment (from laptops to coffee machines).

基础设施就像组织的骨架；你得靠它站直。它包括你所有的技术成本（遗憾的是，云并不是由云做的，更不是棉花糖做的）、物理空间（如果你还有办公室的话），以及设备（从笔记本电脑到咖啡机）。

All these services make modern business possible—from software subscriptions to key SaaS platforms ranging from customer relationship management tools to observability platforms, recruitment tools, professional services like lawyers and accountants, and specialized security and data analysis support.

所有这些服务让现代商业成为可能——从软件订阅，到关键的 SaaS 平台（从客户关系管理工具到可观测性平台）、招聘工具、律师和会计师等专业服务，以及专门的安全和数据分析支持。

— 原书第 152 页 —

Headcount Planning and Costs

人头编制规划与成本

When we talk about people costs being your biggest line item, let’s get specific about what that really means. Headcount planning isn’t just about salaries; it’s about understanding the full cost of a human being in your organization and planning for the complex dynamics of team growth.

当我们说人力成本是你最大的支出项时，让我们具体说说这到底意味着什么。人头编制规划不只是工资；它是要理解一个人在你组织里的完整成本，并为团队成长的复杂动态做好规划。

The real cost of a person. When you’re budgeting for headcount, the salary is just the beginning. In our experience, the “fully loaded cost” of an employee typically runs 1.3–1.8 times their base salary, depending on your location and benefits package. Here’s what you’re actually paying for:

一个人的真实成本。做人头预算时，工资只是个开头。根据我们的经验，一名员工的“全负荷成本”通常是基本工资的 1.3–1.8 倍，具体取决于你所在地区和福利套餐。你实际在为以下这些东西买单：

  • Base salary. The number everyone focuses on.

    基本工资。所有人盯着看的那个数字。

  • Payroll taxes and government mandates. Social Security, Medicare, and unemployment insurance (roughly 7.65% in the US, but this varies by country).

    工资税与法定缴费。社保、医疗保险、失业保险（在美国大约是 7.65%，各国不同）。

  • Benefits. Health insurance, retirement contributions, life insurance (can be 20–30% of base salary).

    福利。医保、退休缴款、人寿保险（可达基本工资的 20–30%）。

  • Equipment. Laptops, monitors, software licenses ($5,000–$10,000 annually for engineers).

    设备。笔记本、显示器、软件许可证（工程师每年 5,000–10,000 美元）。

  • Office space and utilities. Even in remote setups, you might provide stipends.

    办公场地与水电。即便远程办公，你也可能要发补贴。

  • Training and development. Conferences, courses, books ($2,000–$5,000 per person annually).

    培训与发展。会议、课程、书（每人每年 2,000–5,000 美元）。

  • Recruiting costs. Whether agency fees (15–25% of base salary) or internal recruiter time.

    招聘成本。不管是猎头费（基本工资的 15–25%）还是内部招聘人员的时间。

  • Onboarding inefficiency. Considering that new hires typically operate at 50% productivity for their first three months.

    入职低效。要考虑新人头三个月通常只有 50% 的产出。

These stats are based on recent data from the IRS.

这些数据基于美国国税局（IRS）的近期资料。

— 原书第 153 页 —

In Practice: April’s Story

实战：April 的故事

At PixelCurl, April learned this the hard way. She budgeted for three new engineers at $150,000 each, thinking she needed $450,000 in total. However, the actual cost came closer to $675,000 when she factored in everything, and that’s before considering the senior engineer’s time lost to mentoring and onboarding.

在 PixelCurl，April 是吃了苦头才学到这一课的。她按每人 150,000 美元预算招三个新工程师，以为总共要 450,000 美元。然而把所有因素算进去后，实际成本接近 675,000 美元——这还没算高级工程师花在带人和入职上损失的时间。

Planning for growth and attrition. Your headcount plan also needs to account for both growth and natural turnover. Industry average attrition for engineering teams runs 10–15% annually, though it can spike higher in hot job markets or drop lower in economic downturns. This means that for a 20-person team, you should budget to replace two or three people per year just to maintain current capacity.

为增长与流失做规划。你的人头计划既要考虑增长，也要考虑自然流失。工程团队的行业平均年流失率在 10–15% 之间，不过在热门就业市场会更高，在经济下行期会更低。这意味着一个 20 人的团队，光是维持现有产能，每年就得预算替换两三个人。

When planning for growth, consider the rule of temporary productivity loss: every new hire temporarily reduces team productivity before increasing it. The team spends time interviewing, onboarding, mentoring, and context sharing. A good rule of thumb is that adding a new person reduces team capacity by 10% for their first month, 5% for their second month, and then becomes additive in the third month.

规划增长时，要考虑“临时生产力损失”这条规律：每个新人在提升团队生产力之前，都会先短暂拉低它。团队要花时间面试、入职、带教、同步上下文。一个好用的经验法则是：加一个新人，第一个月团队产能降 10%，第二个月降 5%，到第三个月才开始正向贡献。

Timing your hires. The timing of headcount additions can make or break your budget. Consider the following:

把控招聘时机。什么时候加人，直接决定你的预算是成是败。请考虑以下几点：

  • Seasonal patterns. Hiring in Q4 is often harder and more expensive due to holidays and bonus cycles.

    季节性规律。因为假期和奖金周期，第四季度招人通常更难、更贵。

  • Batch versus continuous hiring. Hiring three engineers at once creates an onboarding bottleneck, but it might be more efficient for recruiter time.

    批量招聘 vs. 持续招聘。一次招三个工程师会造成入职瓶颈，但对招聘人员的时间可能更高效。

  • Ramp time aligned with project needs. If you need someone productive for a project in Q3, you should be hiring in Q1.

    爬坡时间与项目需求对齐。如果你需要某人在第三季度的项目上出活，那第一季度就该开始招。

  • Budget cycle alignment. Many companies approve headcount annually; missing your window might mean waiting another year.

    与预算周期对齐。很多公司一年才批一次人头；错过这个窗口可能就得再等一年。

— 原书第 154 页 —

In Practice: April’s Story

实战：April 的故事

When April built her StudioOps headcount budget, she allocated funds across three scenarios: best case (all new hires start within Q1 and ramp quickly), expected (staggered hiring with normal ramp time), and worst case (where difficulty finding DevOps talent means extending the timeline and requires contractor support). She specifically budgeted for onboarding costs that previous leaders had overlooked: mentor time allocation, training resources, and the productivity dip that occurs during knowledge transfer.

April 做 StudioOps 人头预算时，按三种情景分配资金：最佳情况（所有新人第一季度内入职并快速爬坡）、预期情况（错峰招聘、正常爬坡）、最差情况（找不到 DevOps 人才，导致 timeline 拉长、需要承包商支持）。她还专门为前几任领导忽视的入职成本做了预算：导师的时间分配、培训资源，以及知识传递期间出现的生产力下滑。

Seniority mix and team balance. Additionally, not all headcounts are created equal. A senior engineer might cost twice as much as a junior, but doesn’t necessarily provide twice the value—sometimes more, sometimes less, depending on your needs. Consider your team’s pyramid, as shown in Table 7-1. (These salary figures are estimates rather than hard and fast bands.)

资历结构与团队平衡。另外，人头和人头并不一样。一个高级工程师的成本可能是初级的两倍，但未必提供两倍的价值——有时更多，有时更少，取决于你的需求。请参考表 7-1 所示的团队金字塔。（这些薪资数字是估算，而非硬性区间。）

The ideal ratio varies by company stage and needs. Startups might skew senior-heavy for speed, while established companies might invest more in juniors for long-term growth.

理想比例因公司阶段和需求而异。创业公司可能为了速度而偏“高级重”，成熟公司则可能为了长期成长而更多投资初级工程师。

In Practice: April’s Story

实战：April 的故事

For example, April’s challenge at PixelCurl is that her senior-heavy team lacks the middle layer that typically helps juniors grow, forcing seniors into mentorship roles they aren’t prepared for.

举个例子，April 在 PixelCurl 面临的挑战是：她那个“高级重”的团队缺少中间层——而中间层通常正是帮初级工程师成长的人——结果高级工程师被迫承担他们毫无准备的带教角色。

Hidden costs and failure scenarios. Budget for hiring failures because not every hire works out, and the cost of a bad hire can be two to three times their annual salary when you factor in opportunity cost, team disruption, and replacement costs. You should build in contingency for failed hires. For example, we typically budget 10–15% extra to account for the possibility of hiring mistakes, as well as extended search times. For example, key roles might take three to six months to fill. Can you afford to hire contractors in the meantime?

隐性成本与失败情景。要为招聘失败做预算，因为不是每次招聘都成。把机会成本、团队扰动和替换成本算进去，一次错误招聘的代价可能是该员工年薪的两到三倍。你应当为失败的招聘预留应急。比如，我们通常多预算 10–15%，以应对招聘失误以及招聘周期拉长。关键岗位可能要花三到六个月才能招到。这段时间你雇得起承包商吗？

— 原书第 155 页 —

Candidates will often make counteroffers, or you may be competing against other opportunities. For this, you might need to go 10–20% above the initial budget to land critical talent. Finally, consider retention adjustments. Keeping your existing team might require mid-cycle adjustments, or if a key resource receives an offer, you may need to consider establishing a rainy-day fund for counteroffers.

候选人常常会收到反向 offer，或者你可能正在和其他机会竞争。为此，你可能需要在初始预算之上再加 10–20% 才能拿下关键人才。最后，考虑留任调整。留住现有团队可能需要在周期中途做调整；如果某个关键资源拿到了外部 offer，你可能需要考虑设立一笔应对反向 offer 的应急基金。

The headcount business case. Finally, when requesting a headcount, always frame it as an investment, not a cost. Focus on the impact of the new employee. Will they improve revenue? You should be able to answer with, “This engineer will enable features that drive $X in revenue.” There’s also potentially an opportunity cost: “Delaying this hire means pushing the product launch by X months.” In some cases, you can present adding people as cost avoidance: “Without this DevOps hire, we’ll spend $X on contractors and outages because we’ll continue to have this unstable platform.” Lastly, consider team health, morale, and retention. If you have people burnt out or on the verge of burnout, then adding headcount might not only provide capacity but stop loss. This could be justified by saying, “Current overtime rates are unsustainable and risk losing existing team members.”

人头编制的商业论证。最后，申请人头时，永远把它包装成投资，而不是成本。聚焦新员工带来的影响。他们会提升收入吗？你应当能这样回答：“这位工程师将支撑起能带来 $X 收入的功能。”这里还可能存在机会成本：“推迟这次招聘意味着产品发布延后 X 个月。”在某些情况下，你可以把加人表述为“成本规避”：“如果不招这个 DevOps，我们的平台继续不稳定，就得在承包商和宕机上花 $X。”最后，考虑团队健康、士气和留任。如果有人已经 burnout 或濒临 burnout，那么加人头可能不只是补充产能，更是止损。你可以这样论证：“当前的加班强度不可持续，有失去现有团队成员的风险。”

Remember that headcount is simultaneously your biggest expense and your greatest asset. Plan thoughtfully, budget comprehensively, and always consider the full lifecycle cost of a hire—from recruiter to resignation. The numbers might seem daunting, but understanding them helps you make informed decisions about when, who, and how to grow your team.

请记住：人头既是你最大的开支，也是你最大的资产。审慎规划、全面预算，并始终考虑一次招聘的完整生命周期成本——从招聘人员接触到员工离职。这些数字看着吓人，但理解它们能帮你就“何时、招谁、怎么扩张团队”做出知情决策。

Setting Goals That Make Sense

设定合理的目标

We’ve discussed goal setting earlier in the book, and every goal or program you have defined will likely need a budget, either in terms of people or resources. We’re not going to dive into goals in any depth (see Chapter 5 for that), but goals need to be backed by investments. Again, if you have goals that don’t align with how you spend your budget, you must create that alignment before committing to things you can’t pay for. Budget goals also need metrics; some goals will be absolute numbers (e.g., “reach $10 million in revenue”), while others might be relative (e.g., “grow faster than the market”). The key is to ensure that these goals align with your overall strategy and capabilities.

本书前面讨论过目标设定，你定义的每个目标或计划，大概率都需要一份预算——无论是人力还是资源。我们不打算深入展开目标（那请看第 5 章），但目标必须有投资做后盾。再说一遍：如果你的目标和你花钱的方式对不上，那在承诺那些你付不起的事情之前，你必须先把这种对齐建立起来。预算目标也需要指标；有些目标是绝对数字（比如“收入达到 1,000 万美元”），另一些可能是相对的（比如“增速快于市场”）。关键是确保这些目标与你的整体战略和能力对齐。

Remember: goals should be like good coffee—strong enough to get you moving, but not so strong that they give you anxiety. They should push you to improve while remaining achievable with focused effort.

请记住：目标应该像一杯好咖啡——浓到能让你动起来，但又不至于浓到让你焦虑。它们应当推着你进步，同时在集中投入下仍然可以达成。

— 原书第 156 页 —

Creating Your Budget Template

创建你的预算模板

Your budget must be both detailed enough to be helpful and straightforward enough for people to use. It should show your costs (and potentially your income) and be flexible enough to update as things change. It is a living document that helps guide decisions rather than restrict movement.

你的预算必须既足够详细以提供帮助，又足够简单以便人们使用。它应当展示你的成本（可能还有收入），并且足够灵活，能随情况变化而更新。它是一份活文档，帮你指导决策，而不是捆住你的手脚。

Now we need to populate all of this into a spreadsheet. If you have one, your finance team might provide a template, but just in case, we’re providing one in Figure 7-1 to get you started.

现在我们要把这些内容填进电子表格。如果你公司有模板，财务团队可能会提供；但以防万一，我们在图 7-1 里给了一个，帮你起步。

Insert your fixed and variable costs, including people, into the spreadsheet. The template breaks down costs monthly. This is typically how most folks track spending: short enough to be flexible, long enough to identify meaningful trends. You may or may not have to consider income. It’s unlikely. Forecasting and measuring are generally finance functions that work with sales and marketing. It’s included in our example template, but you can remove it if it’s irrelevant.

把你的固定和变动成本——包括人力——都填进电子表格。模板按月份拆解成本。这通常是大多数人追踪开支的方式：时间够短以保持灵活，又够长以识别有意义的趋势。你可能需要、也可能不需要考虑收入——大概率不需要。预测和度量通常是财务部门与销售、市场协作的职能。我们的示例模板里包含了它，但如果和你无关，删掉即可。

We usually prepare three variant budgets for different scenarios. One for the best case, one for the expected outcome, and one for the worst case. This is contingency planning because, let’s be honest, something always goes wrong (or occasionally goes amazingly well). That’s why we need contingency planning. This isn’t about being

我们通常为不同情景准备三套预算变体：一套最佳情况、一套预期结果、一套最差情况。这就是应急计划——因为说实话，总会出点岔子（或者偶尔好得出乎意料）。所以我们才需要应急计划。这不是悲观，而是有备无患。

— 原书第 157 页 —

pessimistic; it’s about being prepared. We need to consider specific risks, such as what happens if your largest customer leaves, and general uncertainties, like economic downturns. The key is having plans for different scenarios: best-case, worst-case, and “well, that was unexpected” scenarios.

（接上文）我们要考虑具体风险——比如最大客户走了怎么办——以及一般性的不确定性，比如经济下行。关键是为不同情景都备好计划：最佳情况、最差情况，以及“哎呀，这可真没想到”的情况。

Tracking and Managing

追踪与管理

Creating a budget is just the first step; now we need to manage it effectively. We generally recommend reviewing your significant costs, particularly headcount, every month. Cloud services are an excellent example; tracking your spending monthly is a good cadence that should identify trends. Additionally, most cloud platforms have tools to set budgets and alert you to variances. We aim to conduct quarterly strategic reviews that examine the broader picture, typically with the entire organization. We usually produce a new budget annually.

做预算只是第一步；现在我们要有效地管理它。我们一般建议每个月复盘一次重大成本，尤其是人头。云服务就是个绝佳例子：按月追踪开支是一个很好的节奏，足以识别趋势。此外，大多数云平台都有工具可以设定预算、在出现偏差时提醒你。我们的目标是每季度做一次战略复盘，看大局，通常是全组织一起。新预算通常每年做一次。

When actual numbers don’t match the plan (and they never do), we must understand why. This isn’t about pointing fingers; it’s about learning and adapting. We need to look for price variances that tell us if something cost more than expected, volume variances that show if we used more or less than planned, timing differences that indicate whether we spent money sooner or later than expected, and efficiency impacts that reveal whether we’re getting more or less bang for our buck.

当实际数字和计划对不上时（而它们永远对不上），我们必须搞清楚为什么。这不是为了指责任何人，而是为了学习和适应。我们要找价格差异（告诉你某项东西是否比预期贵）、数量差异（显示我们用得比计划多还是少）、时间差异（表明我们比预期早花钱还是晚花钱），以及效率影响（揭示我们的钱花得值还是不值）。

Once you have identified a positive or negative variance, share it. Hiding cost overruns is never successful; it is much better to face that head on. In your organization, different people also need different levels of detail in financial communications. Your leadership will generally want a big-picture view that tells them managers need specific information about their departments to ensure we’re on track. Team leaders require project-level details that enable them to make informed day-to-day decisions. The key is presenting information in a way that’s useful for each audience without overwhelming them with irrelevant details.

一旦发现正偏差或负偏差，就分享出来。掩盖超支从来没有好下场；直面它要好得多。在你的组织里，不同的人在财务沟通上需要不同粒度的信息。你的领导层通常想要大局观；经理们则需要关于自己部门的具体信息，以确保我们没走偏。团队负责人需要项目级细节，才能做出知情的日常决策。关键是以对每个受众都有用的方式呈现信息，而不是用无关细节把他们淹没。

We need to be flexible but not chaotic when handling budget changes. This means having transparent processes for minor adjustments, such as transferring funds between line items, making major changes in response to significant market shifts, and responding to unforeseen events in an emergency.

处理预算变更时，我们需要灵活，但不能混乱。这意味着要有透明的流程来应对小幅调整（比如在不同预算项之间调拨资金）、应对重大市场变化而做的大改，以及在紧急情况下响应突发事件。

Learning from Experience

从经验中学习

After each budget cycle, we need to learn from what happened. What worked well that we should keep doing? What failed that we should avoid next time? What surprised us that we should prepare for in the future? Most importantly, what did we learn that can help us do better next time? It’s about continuously improving how we plan and manage our resources.

每轮预算周期结束后，我们都要从发生的事情中学习。哪些做得好、应该继续？哪些失败了、下次要避免？哪些出乎我们意料、将来要为此做好准备？最重要的是：我们学到了什么，能帮下次做得更好？这关乎持续改进我们规划和管理资源的方式。

— 原书第 158 页 —

The goal isn’t to predict the future perfectly; it’s to have a plan that helps you make better decisions and adapt when things change. Because things will change, as they always do. The best budget enables you to achieve your goals while being flexible enough to adapt when reality doesn’t match your plans. And reality never matches even the best plans, so we keep learning and adjusting as we go.

目标不是完美预测未来；而是有一份计划，帮你做出更好的决策，并在情况变化时灵活适应。因为事情总会变——向来如此。最好的预算能让你达成目标，同时又足够灵活，在现实和计划不符时做出调整。而现实永远和最好的计划对不上，所以我们一边走一边学、一边调整。

Vendor Management

供应商管理

Let’s discuss something that might not sound exciting but can make or break your organization: vendor management. In today’s world, we’re all connected like a giant web of business relationships. Gone are the days when vendors were just people who sold you stuff; now, they’re strategic partners who can either propel you forward or hold you back.

我们来聊一个听起来可能不刺激、却能决定你组织生死的话题：供应商管理。在当今世界，我们都像一张巨大商业关系网中的节点。供应商只是“卖你东西的人”的日子早已过去；如今，他们是战略伙伴——要么推你一把，要么拖你后腿。

The Great Build-Versus-Buy Debate

著名的“自研还是采购”之争

Build-versus-buy is the art of identifying what to build as opposed to what to buy. We always focus on what we call “core business,” which normally means building the things that provide a business edge or competitive advantage and not building the things that aren’t core business. Here’s a question that keeps many leaders up at night: should we build it ourselves or buy it from someone else? It’s like the “make dinner or order takeout” decision, but with much bigger stakes. When making this decision, we must consider our core competencies alongside our available resources and time constraints. We also need to think hard about the long-term implications of our choice. Creating a custom solution might seem appealing, but we also create a future maintenance headache that will haunt us for years.

“自研还是采购”，是一门判断“什么该自己造、什么该去买”的艺术。我们始终聚焦所谓“核心业务”，通常意味着：自己造那些能带来商业优势或竞争壁垒的东西，而不去造那些非核心的东西。有个问题让很多领导夜不能寐：这东西该自己造，还是找别人买？这就像“自己做饭还是点外卖”的抉择，只是赌注大得多。做这个决策时，我们必须在核心能力之外，同时考虑可用资源和时间约束。我们还要认真想清楚这个选择的长期后果。做一个定制方案可能很诱人，但你同时也给自己挖了一个未来好几年都甩不掉的维护大坑。

In Practice: April’s Story

实战：April 的故事

April faced this decision with PixelCurl’s deployment pipeline. The StudioOps team had historically maintained a tailored customer improvement/customer development (CI/CD) system that was built by two senior engineers years ago. It consumes 20% of their time just for maintenance. April recognized that deployment pipelines weren’t PixelCurl’s competitive advantage: their innovative animation rendering engine was. She made the strategic call to migrate to a commercial CI/CD platform, freeing those senior engineers to mentor juniors on the actual core business.

在 PixelCurl 的部署管线上，April 就面对过这个抉择。StudioOps 团队多年来自行维护一套定制的 CI/CD 系统，是当年两位高级工程师搭起来的。光维护它就要吃掉他们 20% 的时间。April 意识到，部署管线并不是 PixelCurl 的竞争优势——他们创新的动画渲染引擎才是。她做出战略决策：迁移到商业 CI/CD 平台，把那两位高级工程师解放出来，去带初级工程师做真正的核心业务。

Just because we can build something doesn’t mean we should. Sometimes, the best technical solution isn’t the best business solution. We need to be honest about our capabilities and limitations. Building in-house means committing to ongoing maintenance, updates, and support; it’s not just about the initial development.

能自己造，不代表就该自己造。有时候最好的技术方案，并不是最好的商业方案。我们要诚实地面对自己的能力和局限。自研意味着承诺持续的维护、更新和支持；它不只是最初那一轮开发。

— 原书第 159 页 —

We always tell people to focus development efforts on core business, where building and owning something provides a business or competitive advantage. If you can buy a commodity service off the shelf, do it. Don’t distract from your core business by building something that doesn’t provide that advantage. This shouldn’t be hard calculus either: creating your own database (unless you’re a database company), your own scheduling system, or your own authentication and encryption are all unnecessary. It should be easy to determine that building these sorts of things is an indulgence, not a requirement.

我们总是告诉别人：把开发精力聚焦在核心业务上——在那里，自研并拥有某样东西能带来商业或竞争优势。如果是能从货架上买到的标准化服务，就买。不要为了造一个不带来优势的东西而分心于核心业务。这道算术题也不该很难：自己造数据库（除非你就是家数据库公司）、自己造调度系统、自己造认证和加密，都是不必要的。应当很容易判断：造这类东西是一种放纵，而不是刚需。

Your vendors are the individuals who will provide those noncore capabilities, so they need to deliver the most effective, cost-efficient, and reliable services. A prime example of this in the technical world is cloud services and SaaS business tools. These have primarily replaced in-house datacenters, specialized software solutions have taken over where custom development once reigned, and external expertise fills the gaps that we can’t (or shouldn’t) fill ourselves. This dependency is both powerful and scary. With most vendors, you’re not just looking for a quick transaction; you’re potentially starting a long-term relationship that requires care, attention, and clear boundaries. Choosing the wrong partner can lead to painful experiences and force you to focus on noncore activities at the expense of your business.

你的供应商就是那些提供非核心能力的人，所以他们必须交付最有效、最划算、最可靠的服务。在技术世界里，云服务和 SaaS 商业工具就是最好的例子。它们基本取代了自建数据中心；专用软件解决方案接管了当年定制开发称王的领地；外部专家则填补了我们自己填不了（或不该填）的空缺。这种依赖既强大又可怕。对大多数供应商而言，你要找的不是一锤子买卖；你很可能是在开启一段长期关系，需要用心经营、持续关注，并划清边界。选错伙伴可能带来痛苦的经历，还会迫使你牺牲业务去关注非核心活动。

Picking Your Partners

挑选你的伙伴

Selecting vendors is like hiring employees, except they come with their own companies attached. We need to look beyond just capabilities and track records. While those are crucial, we must also evaluate their stability and cultural fit. A vendor might have the perfect solution, but if their work style clashes with your culture, the relationship will be an uphill battle from day one.

挑选供应商就像招员工，只不过他们还自带一家公司。我们不能只看能力和过往履历。虽然这些很关键，但我们还必须评估他们的稳定性和文化契合度。一个供应商可能有完美的解决方案，但如果他们的工作方式和你的文化相冲，这段关系从第一天起就是一场爬坡苦战。

You also need to work out your requirements (must-haves versus nice-to-haves), the longevity of the solution (and the vendor) and, importantly, what it costs. Contract negotiation isn’t just about getting the lowest price; it’s about creating a framework for a successful relationship. We need crystal-clear definitions of what we’re getting, how we’ll measure success, and what happens when things go wrong (because they inevitably will). The best contracts don’t try to predict every possible problem but rather establish clear principles and processes for handling whatever comes up.

你还需要理清自己的需求（必须有 vs. 有了更好）、方案（以及供应商）的 longevity，还有——很重要——它要花多少钱。合同谈判不只是为了拿到最低价；而是为一段成功的关系建立框架。我们需要无比清晰地定义：我们到底得到什么、如何衡量成功、以及出了问题怎么办（因为问题迟早会出）。最好的合同不是试图预测每一个可能的问题，而是为“不管出什么事”建立清晰的原则和流程。

Managing the Relationship

管理这段关系

The real work begins once we’ve picked our vendors and signed the contracts. Vendor management requires regular attention, care, and occasional pruning. Along with reviewing performance metrics, regular check-ins offer opportunities to share feedback, discuss upcoming changes, and catch minor issues before they become significant problems. A good vendor relationship should feel like a partnership, not a transaction.

真正的工作，在选好供应商、签完合同之后才开始。供应商管理需要持续的关注、用心，以及偶尔的修剪。除了复盘绩效指标，定期的沟通会还提供了分享反馈、讨论即将到来的变更、在小问题演变成大麻烦之前把它抓住的机会。一段好的供应商关系，应该让人感觉是伙伴关系，而不是一锤子交易。

— 原书第 160 页 —

In Practice: April’s Story

实战：April 的故事

April inherited several vendor relationships at PixelCurl, including an expensive monitoring tool that only one senior engineer is familiar with. She conducted quarterly vendor reviews, where the entire team evaluated whether each tool served the collective needs. This process revealed that three different engineers were unnecessarily paying for similar code analysis tools because they never discussed it with each other—a perfect example of how silos create budget waste.

April 在 PixelCurl 接手了好几段供应商关系，其中包括一个昂贵的监控工具，而全公司只有一位高级工程师熟悉它。她每季度做一次供应商评审，让整个团队评估每个工具是否服务于集体需求。这个过程暴露了：三位不同的工程师因为彼此从不沟通，正在各自付费买着功能类似的代码分析工具——这正是孤岛如何造成预算浪费的完美例证。

Outsourced People and Teams

外包的人与团队

Outsourcing functions is like asking someone else to handle your organization’s relationships; it’s complicated and requires extra care and attention. Outsourcing people functions—whether near-sourcing, outsourcing domestically, or hiring offshore contractors—presents complex challenges and risks that require careful evaluation. When you entrust partners with traditionally managed in-house functions—such as human resources, recruitment, or employee relations—you relinquish control over critical processes that shape your culture and workforce. The partners may not fully understand the company’s values, mission, or culture, which can result in both poor service delivery and erode morale and trust within your internal teams. A common problem is when a partner prioritizes skills fit, compliance, and transactional efficiency over finding individuals who align with the organization or team’s culture and have the potential to grow and develop.

把职能外包出去，就像请别人替你经营组织的人际关系；这事很复杂，需要格外用心。把人力相关职能外包——不管是近岸外包、境内外包，还是雇海外承包商——都带来复杂的挑战和风险，需要仔细评估。当你把 traditionally 在内部管理的职能（比如人力资源、招聘或员工关系）托付给合作伙伴时，你就放弃了对那些塑造你文化和员工队伍的关键流程的控制。合作方可能并不完全理解公司的价值观、使命或文化，这既可能导致服务交付质量差，也会侵蚀内部团队的士气和信任。一个常见问题是：合作方优先看重技能匹配、合规和交易效率，而不是去找那些与组织或团队文化契合、有成长潜力的人。

We always recommend aiming for relationships with partners and the engineers they provide, where those engineers feel like they are part of the team. This differs from an engagement with an agency, where a scoped project is involved. Those relationships have their place, but if you bring on people who will interact with your team, they should be treated like part of the team.

我们始终建议：与合作方及其派出的工程师建立关系时，要让那些工程师感觉自己就是团队的一员。这和与一家代理商签订一个有明确范围的项目合同不同。那类关系有它的位置，但如果你招来的人要和你的团队一起工作，就应当被当作团队的一部分来对待。

In Practice: April’s Story

实战：April 的故事

When April needed to quickly fill the DevOps gap while searching for a permanent hire, she brought in a contractor. Rather than isolating them as “the contractor,” she ensured they attended team standups, participated in architecture discussions, and even paired with junior engineers. This approach paid dividends when the contractor helped to identify a critical infrastructure issue that the siloed senior engineers had missed, proving the value of being more inclusive.

April 在招正式 DevOps 期间需要快速补上缺口，于是请了一位承包商。她没有把人家孤立成“那个外包的”，而是确保对方参加团队站会、参与架构讨论，甚至和初级工程师结对。这种做法后来收到了回报：那位承包商帮着发现了一个关键的基础设施问题——而各自为战的高级工程师们都漏掉了它，证明了更包容的做法是有价值的。

This is why we recommend never outsourcing your core hiring processes. Have the partner find people, but put them through your existing interview process. Don’t just take the first resume off the pile and proceed. Trust, but verify, is the watchword

这就是为什么我们建议永远不要把核心招聘流程外包。让合作方去找人，但要让候选人走你现有的面试流程。别从那一堆简历里抽第一份就直接用。“信任，但要验证”，是从外面引人时的座右铭。

— 原书第 161 页 —

when bringing in people from outside. This also reduces the potential impact on organizational culture. A company’s (and a team’s) culture is built on shared values, informal norms, and personal interactions, which can be disrupted when you bring in people who are perceived as “outsiders” or treated like components in a machine. The golden rule applies strongly here: treat external engineers as you’d like to be treated.

（接上文：“信任，但要验证”是从外面引人时的座右铭。）这也能减小对组织文化的潜在冲击。一家公司（以及一个团队）的文化建立在共同价值观、非正式规范和人际互动之上；当你引入那些被视为“外人”、或被当作机器零件对待的人时，文化就可能被打乱。黄金法则在这里格外适用：你希望别人怎么待你，就怎么待外部工程师。

This also reduces the potential that your team may feel disconnected from decision-making processes or perceive the organization as prioritizing cost savings over their well-being. It reduces the risk that institutional knowledge will reside outside the team in the hands of external folks or that design decisions will be made without a broader organizational context, increasing the risk that you can no longer maintain core capabilities with your team if those people move on. Finally, it also reduces communication barriers, especially with offshore contractors operating in different time zones or cultural contexts.

这也降低了团队与决策过程脱节、或觉得组织把省钱看得比员工福祉更重的风险。它降低了“机构知识留在团队之外、攥在外部人员手里”的风险，也降低了“设计决策脱离更广泛的组织上下文”的风险——而如果那些外部人员走了，你就有再也无法靠自己团队维持核心能力的风险。最后，它还降低了沟通障碍，尤其是当海外承包商处在不同时区或不同文化语境中时。

This is never going to be perfect, but a lot of friction can be reduced by treating everyone equally. We both have one-on-ones and sometimes performance planning discussions with contractors, just like any other member of the team. We also try to balance time zones against collaboration. For example, in a recent role, James had teams located in Ukraine, so we held meetings in the morning Eastern Standard Time, which corresponded to the mid-to-late afternoon in Ukraine, ensuring overlap with the team there and enabling interaction between both groups. It’s often hard to juggle this, but maximizing the time that the teams spend together improves collaboration, communication, and trust.

这永远不可能完美，但一视同仁能消除大量摩擦。我们俩都会和承包商做一对一沟通，有时也做绩效规划讨论，就像对待团队其他成员一样。我们也会在时区和协作之间找平衡。比如，在最近一份工作里，James 的团队分布在乌克兰，于是我们把会议安排在美国东部标准时间上午，对应乌克兰的下午中段到傍晚，确保和那边的团队有重叠时间，让两组人能互动。这种平衡常常很难 juggle，但让团队共处的时间最大化，能改善协作、沟通和信任。

There are also legal, regulatory, and data privacy issues when outsourcing humans. Are they in a jurisdiction that has different privacy or data protection laws? Do you feel comfortable that their company will protect your data, especially if they use their own assets or the company has many clients? This refers to selecting vendors carefully: the security of your data and assets are baseline requirements for choosing a partner.

把人外包出去时，还会涉及法律、监管和数据隐私问题。他们所在的司法管辖区，隐私或数据保护法律是否不同？你能放心他们公司会保护你的数据吗——尤其是当他们使用自己的设备、或者公司同时服务很多客户时？这说的就是要谨慎挑选供应商：你的数据和资产安全，是选择合作方的底线要求。

Outsourced people can offer efficiency and cost benefits, but there are also downsides. A good rule of thumb is that you get what you pay for, so weighing these advantages against the potential drawbacks to culture, employee experience, and compliance is essential. Thoughtful decisions about where you get your people from and how you manage them are key.

外包人力能带来效率和成本上的好处，但也有不利的一面。一个好用的经验法则是：一分钱一分货。所以把这些好处与对文化、员工体验和合规的潜在代价权衡清楚，至关重要。关于“从哪里获得人、以及如何管理他们”的深思熟虑的决策，才是关键。

Ethics

职业道德

Let’s talk about ethics, because running a business isn’t just about making money—it’s about doing it the right way. We’ll be blunt: doing things the right way matters because it’s both the right thing to do and because not doing it right will cost

我们来聊聊职业道德，因为经营一家公司不只是赚钱——而是要用正确的方式赚钱。我们直说吧：把事情做对之所以重要，既是因为它本身就是对的，也是因为做不对会让你付出代价。

— 原书第 162 页 —

you people, reputation and, ultimately, business. We frequently tell the people we’re working with that if you don’t want to do the right thing because it’s the right thing, then at least do the right thing to avoid damaging your brand.

（接上文：做不对会让你付出代价。）代价就是人、声誉，最终是生意。我们经常对共事的人说：如果你不是因为“正确”才想去做正确的事，那至少为了不砸自己的招牌，也去做正确的事吧。

So, what do we mean by ethics? We group this into a few areas: taking care of people by treating people fairly and decently, acting honorably, and communicating transparently in our communities, both internally with our colleagues and externally in our user communities.

那么，我们说的职业道德指什么？我们把它归为几个方面：通过公平体面地待人来照顾人、行事光明磊落，以及在我们的社区里透明沟通——既包括内部与同事之间，也包括外部与用户社区之间。

Taking Care of Our People

照顾好我们的人

Our employees aren’t just resources; they are people with lives, families, and dreams. Our budgeting and management decisions need to reflect that reality. This means ensuring fair compensation that enables people to live with dignity, investing in their development because they need opportunities to grow, and maintaining safe working conditions. Nobody should get hurt making a living.

我们的员工不只是资源；他们是有生活、有家庭、有梦想的人。我们的预算和管理决策必须反映这一现实。这意味着：确保公平的薪酬，让人有尊严地生活；投资于他们的发展，因为他们需要成长的机会；以及维持安全的工作条件。任何人都不该在谋生过程中受伤。

In Practice: April’s Story

实战：April 的故事

April discovered a pay gap in the StudioOps team: the junior engineers, despite their struggles without mentorship, were being paid 30% below market rate with the justification that they’re “learning on the job.” She argued successfully that proper mentorship and fair compensation aren’t mutually exclusive; in fact, underpaying while under-supporting is doubly unethical. Her revised budget included both market-rate adjustments and dedicated mentorship time.

April 在 StudioOps 团队发现了薪资差距：那些初级工程师，尽管在没有带教的情况下苦苦挣扎，薪水却比市场水平低 30%，理由是他们“在工作中学习”。她成功地论证了：恰当的带教和公平薪酬并不互斥；事实上，既压低工资又不给支持，是双倍的不道德。她修订后的预算既包含了向市场水平看齐的调薪，也安排了专门的带教时间。

Being a Good Neighbor

做个好邻居

Our organizations don’t exist in a vacuum. Every decision we make has ripple effects on our communities and environment. Since we have only one planet, we must consider our environmental impact, reflect on how our actions affect our local communities, and take responsibility for giving back in meaningful ways.

我们的组织并非存在于真空里。我们做的每个决策，都会在社区和环境中激起涟漪。既然我们只有一个地球，就必须考虑自己的环境影响、反思我们的行为如何影响本地社区，并以有意义的方式承担起回馈的责任。

The Global Perspective

全球视角

In our interconnected world, we must navigate different cultural expectations with care and respect. What’s expected in one place might be inappropriate in another, but we still need to maintain consistent ethical standards across our operations. This means respecting local customs while ensuring fair labor practices and ethical behavior everywhere we operate.

在这个互联互通的世界里，我们必须带着审慎和尊重去应对不同的文化期待。在一个地方被期待的事，在另一个地方可能并不合适；但我们仍需在所有业务中维持一致的道德标准。这意味着：尊重当地习俗，同时在我们运营的每一处都确保公平的劳动实践和合乎道德的行为。

— 原书第 163 页 —

Looking to the Future

展望未来

Ethics aren’t static—new challenges emerge constantly. The rise of artificial intelligence and automation raises new questions about intellectual property, responsibility, and accountability. Data privacy concerns grow more complex as technology advances. Sustainability becomes increasingly crucial as we face global environmental challenges. We need to stay ahead of these issues, thinking beyond the next quarter to consider the long-term implications of our decisions.

职业道德不是静态的——新挑战不断涌现。人工智能和自动化的兴起，带来了关于知识产权、责任和问责的新问题。随着技术进步，数据隐私问题变得愈发复杂。面对全球环境挑战，可持续性变得越来越关键。我们需要走在这些问题前面，思考要超越下一个季度，去考虑决策的长期影响。

Making It Real

落到实处

Ethical principles are great, but they must be more than words on a wall. We need to regularly train our people in ethical decision making and create an environment where people feel safe speaking up when something’s wrong. James worked at Microsoft, where a comprehensive program explained exactly what Microsoft expects from employees and provided articulated scenarios to demonstrate these expectations. Everyone in the organization was fully aware of their obligations and knew what to do if they observed unethical behavior. Many companies provide this training, and you can select a vendor with an appropriate program. This means learning from our mistakes and adapting our approaches as new challenges arise.

道德原则很好，但它们不能只是墙上的标语。我们需要定期培训员工做道德决策，并创造一种环境，让人们在发现不对劲时敢放心开口。James 在微软工作过，那里有一套完整的培训项目，清楚地解释微软对员工的期待，并给出具体场景来演示这些期待。组织里每个人都清楚自己的义务，也知道如果观察到不道德行为该怎么做。很多公司都提供这类培训，你也可以选一家有合适项目的供应商。这意味着从错误中学习，并随着新挑战的出现调整我们的做法。

Remember: ethical behavior isn’t just a nice-to-have but is essential for long-term success. In today’s connected world, our organizations are only as strong as our weakest relationship and our smallest ethical lapse. While we can’t be perfect, we can strive for continuous improvement and conscious decision making. When in doubt, we should ask ourselves: would we be proud to have this decision on the front page of tomorrow’s newspaper? If the answer is no, it’s probably time to rethink things.

请记住：合乎道德的行为不是锦上添花，而是长期成功的必需品。在今天这个互联互通的世界里，我们组织的强度，取决于我们最弱的一段关系和最小的一次道德疏漏。我们无法做到完美，但可以追求持续改进和清醒的决策。拿不准的时候，我们应该问自己：这个决策如果登上明天报纸的头版，我们会感到自豪吗？如果答案是否定的，那大概就该重新想想了。

Conclusion: Budget as Strategy

结语：预算即战略

In this chapter, we’ve navigated the often-unfamiliar territory of budgeting, costs, and vendor management for engineering leaders. We’ve seen that budgeting isn’t just a financial exercise but a strategic tool that helps align your resources with your organization’s goals. The bridge connects your grand visions to practical reality, enabling you to anticipate challenges, seize opportunities, and make informed decisions about your team’s future.

在本章，我们一同探索了工程领导通常并不熟悉的领域：预算、成本和供应商管理。我们看到，预算不只是一场财务操练，而是一个战略工具，帮你把资源与组织目标对齐。这座桥把你的宏大愿景连接到实际现实，让你能够预判挑战、抓住机会，并就团队的未来做出知情决策。

We explored the nuances of cost management, understanding the difference between fixed costs (your organizational foundation) and variable costs (your flexibility factors), and how step-up costs can surprise you when you level up. We discussed the importance of tracking who pays for what and building a culture that considers costs as part of the decision-making process.

我们探究了成本管理的细微之处：理解固定成本（你的组织地基）和变动成本（你的灵活因子）之间的区别，以及当你升级时阶梯成本如何突然给你来一下。我们讨论了追踪“谁为什么买单”、以及建立一种把成本纳入决策过程的文化的重要性。

— 原书第 164 页 —

The budget creation process might seem daunting, but starting with historical data, categorizing expenses thoughtfully, setting sensible goals, and having a flexible template can make it manageable. Remember, the goal isn’t perfection; it’s having a living document that guides decisions and adapts as circumstances change.

创建预算的过程可能让人望而生畏，但从历史数据出发、周到地给支出分类、设定合理的目标、再备一个灵活的模板，就能让它变得可驾驭。请记住：目标不是完美，而是拥有一份活文档，指导决策并随环境变化而调整。

Vendor management is also critical, with the ever-present build-versus-buy debate at its center. We emphasized focusing your development efforts on the core business, where you gain a competitive advantage while partnering with vendors for everything else. When outsourcing people and teams, we highlighted the importance of treating external engineers as part of the team to preserve culture and knowledge.

供应商管理同样关键，其核心是无处不在的“自研还是采购”之争。我们强调把开发精力聚焦在核心业务上——在那里你能获得竞争优势——其他一切则与供应商合作。在把人和团队外包时，我们强调了把外部工程师当作团队一员来对待的重要性，以保护文化和知识。

Finally, we touched on ethics—doing the right thing, not just because it’s right, but because it makes good business sense. Taking care of our people, being good neighbors, maintaining consistent ethical standards globally, and anticipating future challenges are all part of creating an organization that stands the test of time.

最后，我们谈了职业道德——做正确的事，不只是因为它正确，还因为它在商业上是明智的。照顾好我们的人、做个好邻居、在全球维持一致的道德标准、预判未来的挑战——这些都是创建一家经得起时间考验的组织的一部分。

Budgeting, costs, and vendor management might not have drawn you to engineering leadership, but excelling in these aspects will give you the foundation to deliver on the technical vision that did. By bringing the same rigor and thoughtfulness to these business problems that you bring to technical ones, you create the conditions for your team and your organization to thrive.

预算、成本和供应商管理，可能并不是吸引你走上工程领导之路的原因；但在这些方面做到出色，会给你打下地基，让你去交付真正吸引你的那个技术愿景。把你对待技术问题时同样的严谨和深思，带到这些业务问题上，你就为你的团队和组织创造了蓬勃生长的条件。

It’s also a skill you’ll use more and more as you grow your career, both as a leader and as a more senior individual contributor. When we first started in the industry, neither of us ever imagined spending the amount of time we now spend caring about budgets and vendors. We both now lead technical and product teams, but these skills have been crucial even when we’ve dipped back into being senior individual contributors. To build good software, you need a holistic view of how that software is built, including what it costs.

随着你职业生涯的成长——无论是作为领导，还是作为更资深的个人贡献者——这项技能你会用得越来越多。我们刚入行时，谁也没想过自己如今会花这么多时间操心预算和供应商。我们现在都带技术和产品团队，但即便偶尔重新当回资深个人贡献者，这些技能也一直至关重要。要做出好软件，你需要对“软件是怎么造出来的、它要花多少钱”有一个全局视角。

In Chapter 8, we’ll introduce you to technical strategy and how to use it to drive execution and direction.

在第 8 章，我们会向你介绍技术战略，以及如何用它来推动执行和方向。
